$comment: Employee-COUNT-triggered legal obligations for a New York employer -- NOT wage or tax figures, and NOT wired into this engine's calculate() path. See this folder's own README for full scope, and data/minimum-wage/states/NY-2026.json's own employer-SIZE-tier machinery (none exists for NY's minimum wage itself) for the different, narrower kind of size question that IS sometimes machine-readable elsewhere in this project.

thresholds.law: N.Y. Lab. Law 196-b (Paid Sick Leave Law)
thresholds.counts: Employees anywhere the employer operates (not just NY), counted for the PRIOR calendar year -- and a fourth test, net income, that has nothing to do with headcount at all.

tiers.condition: net income <= $1,000,000 in the prior tax year
net income > $1,000,000 in the prior tax year

thresholds.note: The only NY employee-count law in this file whose smallest tier depends on a SECOND, non-headcount test (net income) -- a 3-employee employer's obligation genuinely cannot be answered from headcount alone.

sources.title: N.Y. Labor Law 196-b
sources.verifiedBy: Found via search this session (statutory text, not the NY DOL's own summary page).

sources.title: NY.gov -- New York State Paid Sick Leave FAQ
sources.verifiedBy: The state's own FAQ document, surfaced by search; agrees with the statutory text on all four tiers. Not fetched and read directly this session -- title and URL confirmed via search, content cross-checked against two independent compliance summaries (SixFifty, EmployerPass) that both cite the same four tiers.

thresholds.law: N.Y. Workers' Compensation Law Article 9 (Paid Family Leave)
thresholds.counts: N/A -- there is no employee-count floor at all.

tiers.entitlement: Every private employer with 1+ employees working in NY on each of 30 days in a calendar year becomes a covered employer 4 weeks after that 30th day.

thresholds.note: Included deliberately as a CONTRAST to Paid Sick Leave above: two NY leave laws that sound similar have completely different size logic -- one is a 4-tier headcount ladder, the other has no floor at all. Assuming they share a threshold is a real, easy mistake.

sources.title: NY Paid Family Leave -- Private Employer Coverage Requirements
sources.verifiedBy: The state's own Paid Family Leave site, surfaced by search this session (not fetched directly); content cross-checked against a second independent compliance summary (Paychex) agreeing there is no size threshold.

thresholds.counts: Full-time employees in New York State.

employerCoverage.note: Lower than the FEDERAL WARN Act's 100-employee floor -- a NY employer can be covered by state WARN while being too small for federal WARN.

triggeringEvents.description: 25 or more full-time employees laid off, if that represents at least 33% of all employees at the site.
250 or more full-time employees laid off, regardless of what percentage of the site's workforce that represents.
Certain relocations and covered reductions in work hours also trigger notice; NY's own regulations (not re-fetched in full this session) define these further.

thresholds.noticePeriod: 90 days -- 50% longer than the federal WARN Act's 60 days.

sources.title: NY Department of Labor -- Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN)
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched and read directly this session. Source of the 50-employee coverage floor, the 90-day notice period, and the three quoted triggering-event thresholds verbatim.

knownGaps: The exact regulatory definition of a covered 'relocation' or 'reduction in work hours' was not fetched this session -- NY DOL's own WARN fact sheet PDF returned unparseable binary content to the fetch tool used; re-fetch it directly, or consult dol.ny.gov's WARN regulations page, before relying on this entry for those two triggers specifically.

thresholds.counts: Employees, for determining whether the EMPLOYER is small enough for state law to apply (the opposite direction from most thresholds in this file, which turn an obligation ON above a floor -- this one turns state law ON below a ceiling, precisely to cover the employers federal COBRA below leaves out).

tiers.entitlement: Employer's INSURED group health plan must offer up to 36 months of state continuation coverage -- filling the gap federal COBRA (20+ employees) leaves for small employers.

Federal COBRA applies instead (see the federal thresholds below); NY also requires insured plans to extend federal COBRA's own 18/36-month periods further under separate provisions, not modelled here.

thresholds.note: Applies only to INSURED group health plans, not self-insured ones -- a self-insured small employer is covered by neither federal COBRA nor NY's mini-COBRA.

sources.title: NY Department of Financial Services -- COBRA and Premium Assistance
sources.verifiedBy: Found via search this session (not fetched directly); cross-checked against a second independent source (cobrainsurance.com's NY page) agreeing on the <20-employee threshold, the 36-month period, and the insured-plans-only limitation.

thresholds.law: N.Y. Executive Law Article 15 (NY State Human Rights Law)
thresholds.counts: N/A for most claims as of 2020 -- see note.

tiers.entitlement: Covers discrimination, harassment and retaliation claims against employers of ANY size, for claims accruing on or after 2020-02-08.

thresholds.note: Historically limited to employers with 4+ employees; sexual harassment claims were opened to all employers regardless of size in 2018, and 2019 amendments (effective 2020-02-08) eliminated the 4-employee floor entirely for discrimination and retaliation claims generally. A payroll or HR system still gating NYSHRL coverage on a 4-employee test is running six years out of date.

sources.title: Loeb & Loeb -- New York State amends workplace discrimination, harassment and retaliation laws
sources.verifiedBy: Found via search this session; cross-checked against a second independent law-firm summary (Kauff McGuire & Margolis) agreeing on the 2020-02-08 effective date and the elimination of the 4-employee floor.

thresholds.counts: Wages paid, not headcount -- included here because it is the lowest, most-crossed threshold a brand-new NY employer hits, and it is easy to assume (wrongly) that it is headcount-shaped like the others in this file.

tiers.condition: $300 or more in wages paid in ANY calendar quarter
tiers.entitlement: Employer becomes liable for NY unemployment insurance from the FIRST DAY of that quarter, and must register (Form NYS-100).

thresholds.note: Not a headcount test at all -- a single employee earning $300 in a quarter triggers this. Listed here for completeness against the 'how many employees before X applies' framing, but the honest answer for UI is 'one, immediately, if they're paid enough.'

sources.title: NY Department of Labor -- Register for Unemployment Insurance
sources.verifiedBy: Found via search this session (not fetched directly); cross-checked against a second independent payroll-compliance source (Rho) agreeing on the $300/quarter threshold and first-day-of-quarter liability.

thresholds.counts: Annual gross business volume in DOLLARS, not headcount -- the one entry in this file that is a revenue test, included because it is the single most common cause of a mistaken belief that 'small businesses are exempt from minimum wage.'

tiers.entitlement: Enterprise coverage under the FLSA (including its $7.25 federal minimum wage) applies once a business does $500,000+ in annual gross volume.

thresholds.note: This does NOT mean a smaller NY business is unregulated -- an employee individually engaged in interstate commerce is covered regardless of enterprise revenue (29 U.S.C. 206(a)), AND New York's own minimum wage (data/minimum-wage/states/NY-2026.json) has NO revenue or size exemption of its own, unlike Arizona's or Missouri's state minimum wage statutes, which explicitly exempt the same small, non-FLSA-covered businesses. A New York employer under $500,000 in revenue is still bound by the state's $16.00/$17.00 floor either way.

sources.title: data/minimum-wage/federal-2026.json (this engine's own federal minimum wage file)
sources.verifiedBy: Cross-referenced from this engine's own already-verified federal-2026.json standard.coverage field rather than re-researched from scratch.

thresholds.counts: Full-time employees (30+ hours/week or 130+ hours/month) PLUS full-time-equivalents computed from part-timers' hours, averaged over the PRIOR calendar year.

tiers.entitlement: 'Applicable Large Employer' status: must offer minimum essential coverage to at least 95% of full-time employees (and dependents to age 26) or face a penalty.

thresholds.note: 2025's workforce data determines 2026 ALE status -- this is a LOOKING-BACK test, not a real-time one. The 2026 affordability percentage (the maximum share of household income an employee can be charged for the cheapest qualifying plan) is 9.96%.

sources.title: IRS -- Determining if an employer is an applicable large employer
sources.verifiedBy: Found via search this session (not fetched directly); cross-checked against multiple independent ACA-compliance summaries agreeing on the 50-FTE threshold, the FTE-from-part-timers calculation, and the 9.96% 2026 affordability figure.

thresholds.counts: Employees within 75 miles of the worksite -- a GEOGRAPHIC headcount, not a companywide one.

tiers.condition: within a 75-mile radius of the worksite
tiers.entitlement: Employer must provide up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave to eligible employees.

thresholds.note: An employee is separately only ELIGIBLE after 12 months of employment and 1,250 hours worked in the prior 12 months -- employer coverage and employee eligibility are two different tests, both of which must be met.

sources.title: 29 U.S.C. 2611(4)(A)(i)-(ii)
sources.verifiedBy: Statutory citation for the long-stable 50-employees/75-mile and 12-months/1,250-hours figures, not independently re-fetched this session as they have not changed in over a decade.

thresholds.counts: Employees on a typical business day in the prior calendar year.

tiers.entitlement: Group health plan must offer 18-36 months of continuation coverage (length depends on the qualifying event) after a qualifying loss of coverage.

thresholds.note: Below this floor, NY's own mini-COBRA (ny_mini_cobra above) fills the gap for insured plans -- a NY employer is essentially never fully outside SOME continuation-coverage obligation, federal or state, though a small SELF-insured plan can fall through both.

sources.title: U.S. DOL -- COBRA Continuation Coverage
sources.verifiedBy: Statutory citation for the long-stable 20-employee floor, not independently re-fetched this session.

thresholds.law: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; the ADA; the ADEA
thresholds.counts: Employees for each working day in each of 20+ calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year.

tiers.entitlement: Title VII (race/color/religion/sex/national origin) and the ADA (disability) coverage begins.
ADEA (age 40+) coverage begins -- a HIGHER floor than Title VII/ADA, and state/local government employers are covered by ADEA regardless of size.

thresholds.note: New York's OWN Human Rights Law (ny_human_rights_law above) has no size floor at all for the same categories of claim -- a NY employer with 10 employees is outside federal EEO law entirely but fully inside NYSHRL, which is why 'am I covered by anti-discrimination law' cannot be answered by federal law alone for a New York employer.

sources.title: EEOC -- Section 2, Threshold Issues
sources.verifiedBy: Found via search this session (not fetched directly); the 15-employee (Title VII/ADA) and 20-employee (ADEA) figures are long-stable statutory thresholds cross-checked against a second independent legal reference summary.

knownGaps: NYC Human Rights Law's own 4-employee floor, NYC's Fair Chance Act, NYC's Earned Safe and Sick Time Act (which predates and interacts with the state Paid Sick Leave law above), and other NYC-specific thresholds are not researched here -- state and federal only.

'Single employer' / common-ownership aggregation rules -- whether commonly-owned or affiliated companies must be combined to reach a threshold -- are a fact-specific legal test under each individual statute and are not modelled for any entry in this file.

Several primary NY DOL and NY DFS pages were found by search but not fetched and read directly this session (their own binary/PDF format defeated the fetch tool used, or a live fetch was not attempted) -- each such entry's own sources say so explicitly; treat those as cross_source_confirmed via independent legal-compliance summaries, not as independently primary-verified.

This file is a snapshot as of the asOf date above, not a monitored feed the way data/minimum-wage/ is (see harvester/). None of these thresholds are known to have year-over-year adjustment schedules the way minimum wage figures do, but that has not been independently confirmed for every entry.
